Compiled by Fukae Sukehito, Doctor of Medicine and Sake [i.e., Imperial Physician]
Honzo Wamyo [Japanese Names for Materia Medica]
Engraved in spring of the Kansei Hinoe-Tatsu year [1796]

Left page:
Preface to the Engraving of the Honzo Wamyo
The medical administration of our court followed the Tang system: the Imperial Medical Office established Doctors who were charged with teaching students. One of their duties concerned the materia medica, establishing charts, cultivation, and officers for gathering and collecting [medicinal substances]. Furthermore, an imperial decree commanded Fukae Sukehito to compile a book of Japanese names [for these substances].

Right page:

The benevolent governance of the ancient kings, who cherished life and showed humanity toward the people, may truly be called complete and thorough. Yet amid the wars and fires that swept China, the writings of the hundred schools were scattered and lost, and this book too was lost along with them. Those who preserved its table of contents were few, and scholars noted it only briefly. A physician of the inner court happened to come across a transcribed copy in the catalog of the secret imperial library.

Left page:

The Honzo Wamyo in two volumes: a request was made to have it copied and kept. At first it was not known who had compiled it, but upon examining its structure, it was found to follow entirely the arrangement of the Newly Revised Materia Medica compiled by Su Jing of the Tang dynasty, with additions drawn from various household dietary classics and other works cited here and there, so that lost writings from the Sui and Tang dynasties and earlier, along with regional terms and variant species, appear layer upon layer in abundance.

Right page:
Preface to the Honzo Wamyo

There are things that even the Tang scholars Shen Wei and Li Shizhen did not collect. Not only does this work benefit and support the art of medicine, it can also serve as a resource for the broadly learned. That it was composed to supplement the work of Furen is thus abundantly clear. Yet unfortunately, the years and annual rites recorded within span nearly eight hundred years, and having passed through successive copyings, the text became so corrupted and confused that it could no longer be verified or relied upon.

Left page:
Preface to the Honzo Wamyo

Drawing upon such works as the Bencao, the Erya, the Shuowen, the Yupian, the Wamyo Ruijusho from Shuzhou, and the Ishinpo, I collated their agreements and differences, corrected errors and omissions, and achieved a result worth examining. I further petitioned for contributions to have it preserved and transmitted to the world. This book, originating from Shuzhou, was thereafter rarely cited or drawn upon.

Honzo Wamyo — Preface
[Volume] 3

Right page:
Apart from Fujiwara no Shōnagon Iwahito's catalogue of books held at Ninnaji Temple, there are no other recorded references to this work. The eminent predecessors of the Imperial Library were all unable to view it, yet now it has come to light before this humble scholar of later generations — truly remarkable! Ah, that a work of such divine worth should emerge — could there have been some omen of its appearance? Or perhaps

Left page:
it is simply a consequence of the flourishing civilization and fortune of the nation. It is indeed a blessing of the imperial grace and its overflowing glory. I therefore ought to devote my full heart and strength to this task, and yet I cannot help but feel regret that my learning is shallow and my knowledge limited, and moreover that my duties are many and pressing, leaving me no leisure to carefully collate and verify. As for laying out the various texts and checking for omissions and errors — that remains yet to be done.
